stories.headline: At his Grand Island, Nebraska rally, Trump signs an order letting anyone buy tax-free ‘red dye’ diesel
stories.summary: Trump used Monday night’s rally at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island to sign an executive order dropping the off-road requirement for red-dyed diesel, the untaxed fuel normally limited to farm vehicles and machinery. “Tonight I’m going to sign a historic executive order to officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red dye diesel for any reason,” he said, adding that it would save a typical trucker more than $100 per fill-up and help bring down grocery prices. A White House fact sheet says the Transportation, Agriculture, Defense and Treasury secretaries will work to widen access to tax-exempt diesel and encourage states to suspend their own diesel taxes. Diesel has climbed more than 70% since the Iran war began Feb. 28 and hit a record $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22, made worse by Russia’s diesel export ban after Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries. The rally, on the first day of early voting in Nebraska, was aimed at boosting Sen. Pete Ricketts, who faces an unexpectedly strong challenge from independent Dan Osborn.

stories.headline: Trump reverses course: MAGA Inc. will pay for his ‘Patriotic Ads’ instead of taxpayers
stories.summary: After criticism from lawmakers in both parties, Trump said on Truth Social Monday that he and his super PAC will now pay for the campaign-style TV ads promoting his administration that had been running on federal money. “The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” he wrote, adding that he had decided to “do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.” A White House official said MAGA Inc. will cover the public service ads “moving forward” and noted that administrations of both parties have used them. Neither the White House nor the super PAC said whether the government will be paid back for ads that already aired; the ad-tracking firm AdImpact estimates at least $10 million in federal spending so far.

stories.headline: Trump approves an Army firing squad for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, nearly 17 years after the massacre
stories.summary: The administration has approved executing former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, by firing squad, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday. Parnell said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recommended the plan and President Trump approved it, and that the Secretary of the Army will set the time and place. “Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” he wrote. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted at a 2013 court-martial of murdering 13 people and wounding more than 30, and he admitted at trial that he opened fire to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. forces. It would be the military’s first execution of a service member since 1961 and a rare use of a firing squad; the federal government normally uses lethal injection.

stories.headline: Declassified files: the Biden-era FBI tracked Melania and Barron Trump’s travel and monitored Susie Wiles’ calls
stories.summary: Records the White House declassified Monday from “Plasmic Echo,” the classified-documents investigation later run by special counsel Jack Smith, show agents tracked the travel of the former first lady and Barron Trump while planning the 2022 Mar-a-Lago search, then monitored calls by Susie Wiles, now White House chief of staff, with defense lawyers, campaign advisers and journalists. A May 2022 pre-raid checklist told agents to “finalize FBI understanding of FPOTUS/FLOTUS/minor son’s travel,” and a June 1 email said any warrant would be served after Trump left the estate. The files also show FBI Director Christopher Wray got Attorney General Merrick Garland’s sign-off in March 2022 to open a “Sensitive Investigative Matter.” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called it “a disgraceful abuse of government power” and said those responsible must be held accountable. The release comes less than a week after Smith’s contentious Senate Judiciary Committee hearing about his separate Arctic Frost probe.

stories.headline: DOJ sues to strip citizenship from 40 naturalized Americans in what Blanche calls the largest denaturalization push in modern history
stories.summary: The Justice Department has filed lawsuits to revoke the citizenship of 40 naturalized Americans it says got that status unlawfully, part of its crackdown on immigration fraud. The defendants come from China, Afghanistan, Egypt, Pakistan, Venezuela, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and Mexico, and the cases involve acting as an agent of the Chinese government, voluntary manslaughter, sex offenses against minors and fraud. “Today’s announcement marks the largest denaturalization effort in modern history,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said Monday, adding that the defendants “concealed critical facts from the U.S. government and represent serious criminal offenders.” One target, Cuban-born Javier Marrero-Pando of Georgia, is accused of swearing in October 2020 that he had never committed a crime he wasn’t arrested for, months after forcing a man with special needs into sex acts; he later pleaded guilty to aggravated sodomy.

stories.headline: Tom Homan turns the question on CBS over ICE custody deaths: ‘How many people died during the Biden administration?’
stories.summary: In a Friday interview, CBS News immigration correspondent Camilo Montoya-Galvez told border czar Tom Homan that 57 people have died in ICE custody under this administration and that 2026 could set a record. Homan shot back, “How many people died in custody during the Biden administration? Do you know?” After Montoya-Galvez answered “a significant number” and then admitted, “I don’t have the data here,” Homan replied, “Of course you don’t,” calling it “another loaded question against the Trump administration.” Homan said ICE has the highest detention standards in the industry, that deaths are up because the number in custody has roughly doubled to about 74,000, and that ICE doctors often find serious conditions detainees didn’t know they had. “It’s sad when anybody dies,” he said, “but we do everything we can to give them the best medical care.”

stories.headline: Ex-‘American Idol’ singer and pastor Caleb Flynn gets life without parole for murdering his wife
stories.summary: Caleb Flynn, a former “American Idol” contestant and pastor convicted last week of murdering his wife, Ashley, in a killing he tried to blame on an intruder, was sentenced Monday in Ohio to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Flynn, who did not testify at trial, still claimed innocence: “I have unfortunately lied about a lot of things over the last couple of years, but as I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife.” Ashley’s mother, Jill Smith, read a statement from the couple’s 12-year-old daughter, Alyssa: “I love you deeply with all my heart, and it’s sad that you can’t love anyone but yourself.” The girl said confessing was the least her father could do, and added, “by the way, I don’t plan on coming to see you.”

stories.headline: Russian guided bombs kill six and wound 59 in Kharkiv, including three children
stories.summary: Russia struck Kharkiv’s Slobidskyi district Monday afternoon with at least three guided aerial bombs and a combat drone, killing six people and injuring 59, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Thirty-five people suffered blast injuries and the rest had cuts, glass wounds, bruises and shock. Three children were among the wounded: an 11-year-old girl and a 15-year-old boy with blast injuries and a 15-year-old girl in shock. Thirty people remained in the hospital Monday evening, three of them in extremely serious condition, and rescuers later found the body of the sixth victim in the rubble. The bombs hit civilian businesses and landed near a multi-story apartment building, setting off two large fires at a warehouse and an industrial building and damaging high-rises and cars.

stories.headline: Trump says the U.S. will ‘help’ Russia with its plague scare after a Siberian lab worker’s death
stories.summary: Asked by reporters Monday about the plague reports out of Russia, Trump said he was aware of the situation and that the United States will “help them.” “I hate to see them having it; it’s a rough disease,” he said. “We’ll help anybody that has that kind of problem.” Russian officials and media reported on Oct. 4 that an aluminum plant and several hospitals in Irkutsk Oblast had put in quarantines and mask rules after the death of Darya Shipilova, a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov. She reportedly broke a test tube holding the bacterium that causes pneumonic plague while collecting samples about a week earlier and died Oct. 2. Trump’s offer comes as Russia keeps up deadly strikes on Ukrainian cities and Ukraine and its allies push for tougher sanctions.

stories.headline: Judge in the Charlie Kirk murder case tells lawyers to come ready to set Tyler Robinson’s trial dates on Oct. 23
stories.summary: Fourth District Judge Tony Graf has ordered prosecutors and defense attorneys in Tyler Robinson’s capital murder case to be ready at an Oct. 23 hearing to propose a timeline for trial. By Oct. 21 they must file memos estimating how many calendar days they need to prepare, with an itemized list of tasks, how many trial days and hours per day they expect, and how long it will take to seat a jury and alternates, plus separate estimates for a death-penalty phase if it applies. Graf said the schedule will not be binding and can be adjusted. Robinson, 23, was bound over last month on seven charges, including aggravated murder, in the Sept. 10, 2025, shooting of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University, and pleaded not guilty; he faces a possible death sentence. Defense attorney Greg Skordas, who is not involved in the case, predicts a trial may not happen until 2028.

stories.headline: Conservative ‘Humans First’ activists end an 8,000-mile anti–data center bus tour outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters
stories.summary: A tour bus wrapped in farmhouses, grain fields and the words “AI Data Center Revolt” parked beside Anthropic’s headquarters Monday, the last leg of a five-week, 35-plus-stop trip by Humans First, a conservative group chaired by longtime tea party organizer Amy Kremer. The tour ended with visits to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta and Nvidia. “This technology is being shoved down people’s throats,” Kremer said, arguing that AI giants should not build billions of dollars in infrastructure without residents’ input: “That’s not the American way.” Her daughter, senior adviser Kylie Jane Kremer, pointed to the group’s 13-point data center charter calling for community control over siting, no higher electric bills and no use of U.S. data centers for unconstitutional surveillance. “We’re not anti-AI, we’re not anti-tech, we’re not even anti-data center,” she said. Amy Kremer said she rejects the idea that AI could be conscious or have a soul: “Personally, I think it’s demonic.”

stories.headline: Apple opens the App Store to iPhone Duo-optimized apps as the foldable’s launch nears
stories.summary: Apple said Monday evening on its Developer News hub that developers can now submit iPhone Duo-optimized apps and games built with Xcode 27.1, and it released Xcode 27.1 Release Candidate 1 the same day. Apps built or recompiled with Xcode 27.1 will get a badge on their App Store product page telling shoppers they are optimized for iPhone Duo. Apple also said every app and game submitted to App Store Connect will need iPhone Duo screenshots starting in April 2027. Developers can use Device Hub to preview how their apps behave across all of the Duo’s poses and orientations, and Apple posted design guidance and templates to help them get ready for the launch.

stories.headline: Researchers say new Windows malware ‘x47.c’ can use xAI’s Grok to work out how to stay hidden
stories.summary: Qrator Research Labs has flagged a Windows malware kit called x47.c, advertised by a seller using the name WraithTools, that can steal passwords, grab browser cookies, route internet traffic through an infected computer and even burn through a victim’s paid AI credits. The researchers say it can reportedly call xAI’s Grok to help decide how to keep itself running on an infected PC. Qrator based its findings on the seller’s advertising, technical documentation, screenshots and follow-up messages, so the research describes what the malware is built and marketed to do rather than how widely it is infecting computers. The advice for Windows users is the usual: avoid cracked or unknown software, keep systems updated, use strong unique passwords with two-factor sign-in, and run reputable security software.

stories.headline: Canon, Nikon, Sony and Fujifilm bosses lay out four different visions for where cameras go next
stories.summary: In interviews with Japan’s Nikkei, highlighted by PetaPixel on Monday, the heads of the big four camera brands described very different plans. Canon’s Go Tokura said young buyers are driving a compact-camera revival because they enjoy the shooting experience itself, so Canon will weave “style and feel” into a lineup once built around performance and price, and keep expanding its video-focused V Series and lenses that shoot both video and stills. Nikon’s Hiroyuki Ikegami said it is investing in next-generation processors, sensors and video cameras and sees dedicated cameras as a “smartphone + 1” device. Sony’s Kenji Tanaka described “Spatial AI,” using Alpha sensors to build digital twins of the real world for entertainment, while Fujifilm’s Koji Matsumoto said photography has to stay fun and hands-on in ways phones can’t match.

stories.headline: Winnipeg scores three times in the third to hand the Penguins their first loss, 3–2, in Murashov’s season debut
stories.summary: The Penguins fell to 2–1 Monday night at PPG Paints Arena as the Winnipeg Jets rallied for a 3–2 win. Ben Kindel tipped in a goal at 9:27 of the second period, set up by Declan Carlile and Erik Karlsson, for a 1–0 Pittsburgh lead. Winnipeg answered with Alex Iafallo at 4:43 of the third and Adam Lowry at 7:08. Carlile tied it 2–2 at 8:53 with Kindel and Ville Koivunen assisting, but Cole Perfetti scored just nine seconds later, at 9:02, for the winner. Sergei Murashov, making his first start of the season, stopped 30 of 33 shots before being pulled for an extra attacker late, while Clay Stevenson made 29 saves for Winnipeg with Connor Hellebuyck suspended. Evgeni Malkin, who had scored in each of the first two games, was held off the scoresheet. The Penguins now play five of their next six on the road.

stories.headline: Jets’ Braelon Allen runs for 59 yards in Breece Hall’s place, then blames himself for two missed blitz pickups
stories.summary: With Breece Hall out with a quad injury, Braelon Allen started at running back in Sunday’s 23–12 loss in Chicago and ran 14 times for 59 yards on a day the Jets got only 32 offensive snaps; he carried five straight times for 21 yards on the first drive of the second half. Head coach Aaron Glenn said Allen did “a pretty solid job” and that “the run game showed itself, something that wasn’t good the past two games.” On Monday, Allen took the blame for a slow passing game: “I feel like I let the team down. In the first half, I had two errors on blitz pickup.” Center Josh Myers called that “uncharacteristic” of a “really smart football player.” At 1–3, the Jets host 3–1 Cleveland on Sunday, and Glenn said the team takes it “week to week.”

stories.headline: Alice Cooper plays ‘School’s Out’ and two more classics at halftime of Raiders–Chiefs in Las Vegas
stories.summary: Alice Cooper, with longtime guitarist Nita Strauss and drummer Glen Sobel, played a three-song halftime set at Allegiant Stadium on Sunday during the Kansas City Chiefs’ 30–27 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. Backed by members of David Perrico and the Raiders House Band, they ran through “School’s Out,” “I’m Eighteen” and “No More Mr. Nice Guy.” Cooper told the Las Vegas Review-Journal he kept it simple on purpose: “Those are the three that I think everybody picks up on. Everybody sings on ‘Nice Guy’ and ‘School’s Out’.” Strauss posted a clip afterward and said the band will be back in Vegas next month, when Cooper returns in late November for “Welcome To Our Nightmare,” his rock concert-and-illusion show with Criss Angel at Planet Hollywood.

stories.headline: Citi upgrades Harley-Davidson to buy, saying September U.S. sales may be up double digits
stories.summary: Citi analyst James Hardiman upgraded Harley-Davidson to buy from neutral on Monday and raised his price target to $33 from $31, about 34% above Friday’s close, calling the stock “a compelling entry point ahead of third-quarter earnings/guidance” and an “intriguing” 2027 story. He pointed to a turnaround in North American retail sales after a multiyear slump that has cut the stock 41% since the end of 2022: sales rose 14% to 23,800 bikes in the first quarter and 3% to 29,750 in the second, with strength continuing through July and August. Citi’s checks suggest September retail sales may be up by double digits, which Hardiman said would leave Harley “on pace to significantly outperform current expectations.” Harley raised its 2026 retail outlook to 133,500 to 138,500 motorcycles after the second quarter and reports third-quarter results around Oct. 28.

stories.headline: Trumbull plumbing contractor pleads guilty in a kickback scheme that billed Success Village co-op $2.6 million
stories.summary: Richard J. Messina, 54, of Trumbull, pleaded guilty Monday in federal court in Hartford to conspiracy to commit wire fraud in an embezzlement scheme at Success Village Apartments, a 924-unit cooperative in Bridgeport and Stratford. Prosecutors say that from June 2022 to September 2024 his plumbing and heating companies, Umbrella Mechanical and RJM Mechanical, submitted fake or inflated invoices without competitive bidding and sent about 20% of their payments back to the co-op’s general manager, Charles Pitcher, and another person. Success Village paid Umbrella about $2.63 million and RJM about $99,000, and $546,000 was diverted to Pitcher and the other person. Messina agreed to a forfeiture judgment of at least $750,000 and restitution of at least $1.5 million, faces up to 20 years in prison, and is free on $100,000 bond; his business partner Carmine Gentile and Pitcher have already pleaded guilty.

stories.headline: Babylon Bee: Democrats blame USAID cuts for slowing the communist takeover of the West
stories.summary: Satire. With the midterms approaching, the Bee imagines Democrats complaining that Trump’s USAID cuts have badly set back their plans. “We’re still trying, but it’s making it much more difficult,” a fictional Hakeem Jeffries says, promising that if Democrats win back Congress in November they will get their plan for a communist takeover of the West “back on track.” A make-believe Chuck Schumer adds, “We’ll still get it done, eventually,” and the piece closes with Democrats promising that illegal immigration will “resume in full force once they regain power.”
